name: Troubleshoot and repair turbines on site
summary: When a wind turbine stops on a fault that cannot be reset from the operations centre, a two-person technician team drives to it, locks it out, climbs the tower, finds the cause and replaces the failed part so the turbine can run again. The site supervisor ranks the jobs each morning against scheduled service work. High wind, lightning and icing stop climbing, older towers have no elevator, parts that are not in the site store have to come from central stores or the manufacturer, and driving between farms takes a large share of the day. Faults that turn out to be a gearbox, generator, main bearing or blade failure are made safe and passed to the main component exchange process.

baseline.org_archetype: An Alberta-centred listed generator that maintains most of its southern Alberta wind turbines with its own technicians based at site offices near Pincher Creek and Fort Macleod.
baseline.notes: Wind division of about 70 people running roughly 450 turbines on 11 to 12 southern Alberta wind farms commissioned between 1997 and 2021, most of them older 0.66 to 3 MW machines without tower elevators.

trigger: The operations centre hands a non-resettable turbine fault and its corrective work order to the site supervisor or the on-call technician.
end_state: The turbine runs again and the work order is closed with hours, parts and failure cause recorded, or the turbine is left locked out and a main component work request has been raised.

volume.seasonality: More jobs from November to March (icing, cold and stronger winds cause more faults, while short days and high winds limit climbing); summer visits compete with scheduled service.

evidence.note: Organisation file volume. About 135 visits a month come from the monitor workflow (30 percent of 450 fault stops); the rest are return visits after parts arrive and jobs raised from warnings or inspections. Walgern et al. report 3.3 non-resettable failures per onshore turbine per year, which for about 450 turbines gives about 125 failure visits a month.
Follows the fault surges in the monitor workflow; organisation file estimate.

roles.title: Wind turbine technician
roles.department: Wind and storage: southern Alberta wind sites

evidence.note: Organisation file role (38 people; days with weekend on-call). Alberta wind technician wages about 32 to 45 CAD/h in 2021 per the organisation file. Loaded = wage x 1.40 (benefits about 25 percent, overhead about 15 percent), as in the organisation file. Steps record the lead technician's minutes; a second technician works alongside on every climb, so the stated FTE counts both people (about twice the hands-on time).

roles.title: Wind site supervisor
roles.department: Wind and storage: southern Alberta wind sites

evidence.note: Organisation file role (4 people, one per site group). Loaded = wage x 1.40 (benefits about 25 percent, overhead about 15 percent), as in the organisation file. Morning planning, assignment, escalation and weekly work order review.

roles.title: Renewables operations centre operator
roles.department: Wind and storage: renewables operations centre

evidence.note: Organisation file role (8 people covering one 24x7 desk). Loaded = wage x 1.40 (benefits about 25 percent, overhead about 15 percent), as in the organisation file. Remote restart and confirmation at the end of each repair. Not listed for this process in the organisation file.

systems.name: ERP (finance, purchasing and plant maintenance modules)
Hydro, wind and battery SCADA and remote control
Load, price, wind and inflow forecasting models
Document management and engineering drawings repository

resources.name: Two-person wind technician team with service truck

steps.name: Review the fault handover
steps.description: The site supervisor opens the corrective work order the operations centre created in the ERP, reads the fault code, reset attempts and condition note, and checks in SCADA that the turbine is still stopped.

evidence.note: Faults arrive around the clock but the supervisor works extended day hours, so overnight faults wait for the morning unless the on-call technician is called out.

steps.name: Prioritise and assign a technician pair
steps.description: The supervisor ranks the job on the day's plan against other stopped turbines and scheduled service, weighing megawatts lost, the wind forecast and travel between farms, and assigns it to a technician pair in the ERP.

error.defect_description: Job given to a pair without the right skills or parts for the turbine model.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Review fault history and the manual
steps.description: When a pair comes free the lead technician reads the turbine's recent work orders in the ERP, looks at the SCADA trends around the stop and opens the manufacturer's troubleshooting guide for the fault code to plan likely causes and parts.

evidence.note: 16 pairs for about 450 turbines are usually busy with other jobs; waits range from immediate to the next shift or a weekend. Estimate.

steps.name: Gather likely parts and tools
steps.description: The technicians pick the likely spare parts (sensors, relays, pitch batteries, fuses, slip ring brushes) and tools from the site store, record what they take against the work order and load the truck.

error.defect_description: A needed part is not taken or the site stock count is wrong.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Check wind and weather against climbing limits
steps.description: The lead technician checks current and forecast wind speed at hub height, lightning and icing against the company's climbing and hoisting limits before leaving, and decides whether the climb can go ahead today.

control.basis: Company climbing limits from manufacturer manuals: no nacelle access above about 20 m/s, no hoisting above about 10 m/s, no climbing in lightning or with ice on the turbine

evidence.note: Wind speed limits for nacelle access (20 m/s) and hoists (10 m/s) from the source; the share of no-go days in windy southern Alberta is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for safe climbing weather
steps.description: The job is held while the wind stays above the climbing limit or ice remains on the tower; the pair is moved to ground-level work or another farm and the job is picked up on the next suitable day.

evidence.note: Wind speeds are highest in the cold winter months (aif2021); hold durations are the author's estimate for the Pincher Creek area.

steps.name: Drive to the turbine
steps.description: The pair drives the service truck from the site office or the last job to the turbine, over public roads and gravel access roads across leased farmland, opening gates and following landowner access rules.

evidence.note: Farms spread around Pincher Creek, Cowley and Fort Macleod (aif2021); drive times estimated.

steps.name: Hazard assessment and lockout
steps.description: At the base the pair completes the field-level hazard assessment, calls the operations centre to take the turbine out of remote control, applies personal locks and tags to the isolation points and records the permit in the permit system.

error.defect_description: Isolation point missed on the lockout list.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 2 (hazard assessment) and Part 15 (energy isolation); company permit-to-work standard

evidence.note: Work inside turbines only under a written order or permit (source); durations estimated.

steps.name: Climb to the nacelle
steps.description: The technicians put on fall-arrest harnesses, check the ladder safety system and climb the 50 to 80 metre tower by ladder (most older towers have no lift), hauling tools and parts up with the nacelle hoist.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 9 (fall protection) and the company rule of at least two trained climbers with rescue equipment on every climb

evidence.note: Teams of at least two (ii2025); older towers are climbed without elevators (pe2008). Durations estimated.

steps.name: Diagnose the fault
steps.description: The lead technician connects a laptop to the turbine controller, reads the event log, measures signals and inspects the suspect assembly (pitch, converter, yaw, hydraulics, sensors) to find the cause and decide what to replace.

error.defect_description: Wrong root cause; the part replaced does not fix the fault.

next.condition: fault can be fixed with parts on hand
no fault found; settings adjusted and turbine reset locally
main component failure: gearbox, generator, main bearing or blade

evidence.note: Pitch, control and converter systems fail most often onshore (source); branch shares are estimates. The main component share (about 1 percent of visits, about 1.6 a month after repeat diagnoses) is set to match the organisation file's 1 to 5 exchanges a month, 80 percent of which come from repair visits.

steps.name: Replace the part or repair
steps.description: The pair replaces the failed part or repairs the wiring or hydraulic line, following the manufacturer's procedure and torque values, and records the part serial numbers.

error.defect_description: Loose connection or wrong setting left after the repair.

next.condition: near miss or injury during the work

evidence.note: Average technician time on site is 2.7 h for component replacements and about 1.5 h for other corrective work (source); the range here covers the repair itself, with climbing, diagnosis and testing as separate steps.

steps.name: Test run in local control
steps.description: The technicians release the locks needed for the test, run the turbine from the nacelle or base controller through start-up, pitch and yaw tests, and watch for the fault to return.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Descend and remove lockout
steps.description: The pair packs tools and removed parts, climbs down, removes personal locks and tags, closes the permit and calls the operations centre to hand the turbine back to remote control.

error.defect_description: Lock or tag left on, or permit not closed.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 (energy isolation): locks removed only by the workers who applied them

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Restart the turbine remotely and confirm
steps.description: The operations centre operator clears the block in SCADA, restarts the turbine, watches it reach normal power for the wind and marks it available again in the availability record.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Drive back or on to the next job
steps.description: The pair drives back to the site office or on to the next turbine on the day's plan, returning removed parts for repair or scrap to the site store.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Close the work order in the ERP
steps.description: At the end of the day the lead technician types the work done, failure cause code, parts used and hours into the ERP work order and marks it technically complete.

error.defect_description: Missing or generic failure code, or parts not recorded.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Enter hours in timekeeping
steps.description: Each technician enters the hours against the work order number in the time and attendance system, including any call-out or overtime, for the weekly timesheet.

error.defect_description: Hours booked to the wrong work order.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Review and close the work order
steps.description: In the weekly review the supervisor checks completed work orders for a failure code, parts and hours, approves the timesheets and closes the order, or sends it back for missing information.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Make safe and descend
steps.description: Because the needed part is not on hand, the pair leaves the turbine blocked and safe, climbs down, keeps the lockout or closes the permit as the job requires and drives back.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Raise a material request
steps.description: The lead technician raises a material request in the ERP for the part, quoting the manufacturer part number from the parts manual, and flags it urgent when the turbine is down.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the part
steps.description: The turbine stays down while central stores ships the part or buys it from the manufacturer or a supplier; common parts arrive in a day or two, manufacturer-specific parts for older models can take weeks.

evidence.note: Lead times estimated; parts for discontinued older models are often scarce.

steps.name: Make safe, lock the rotor and leave
steps.description: For a main component failure the pair locks the rotor, leaves the turbine isolated, photographs the damage and takes oil samples or readings, then climbs down and drives back.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Raise a main component work request
steps.description: The supervisor writes a work request in the ERP describing the failed component, the evidence and the turbine's state, and sends it with photos to the site manager to start the main component exchange.

error.defect_description: Failure mode described too vaguely for the part order.

evidence.note: Common practice for owner-operated onshore wind sites in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Report a near miss or injury
steps.description: If something goes wrong during the work, a technician reports it to the supervisor at once and enters the near miss or injury in the incident system the same day so the safety team can investigate.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Act requirement to report serious injuries and incidents, and the company incident reporting standard

evidence.note: Share of jobs with a reportable near miss is an estimate.

exceptions.name: Part not on hand
exceptions.description: The pair diagnoses the fault but the part is not on the truck or in the site store; the turbine waits for a material request and a second visit.

exceptions.name: Too windy to climb
exceptions.description: Wind or ice keeps the pair off the tower and the job slips to the next suitable day.

exceptions.name: Main component failure found
exceptions.description: The fault turns out to be a gearbox, generator, main bearing or blade failure; the turbine is isolated and a main component work request is raised.

exceptions.name: Repair does not fix the fault
exceptions.description: The test run shows the fault again and the pair goes back to diagnosis.

benchmarks.unit: hours of technician presence per corrective component replacement, excluding travel and lead times
benchmarks.population: Onshore wind field data, Walgern et al. 2026

evidence.note: Stated in the source; about 1.5 h for other corrective maintenance.

benchmarks.unit: non-resettable failures per turbine per year
benchmarks.population: Onshore wind field data, Walgern et al. 2026 (WMEP: 2.4)

evidence.note: Stated in the source.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from fault handover to work order closed
benchmarks.population: Author's estimate for an owner-operated southern Alberta wind fleet

evidence.note: Most turbines run again within a day of handover; the weekly supervisor review sets the median for closure, and parts waits and windy days set the tail. Not measured.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from handover to turbine running

evidence.note: Same-day or next-day repair for most faults; part waits of days to weeks for about one in five.

pain_points.description: Travel, climbing and making the turbine safe take as long as the repair itself, so each extra visit for a missing part costs a pair half a day.

evidence.note: Repair times of 1.5 to 2.7 h on site exclude travel and lead times (source); the comparison with travel is the author's.

pain_points.description: Windy days, lightning and icing stop climbing in exactly the season when faults are most frequent.

evidence.note: Climbing limits (ii2025) and higher winter wind speeds (aif2021).

pain_points.description: Failure codes and parts are typed into the ERP at the end of the day, often generically, which weakens the failure history the reliability engineers rely on.

evidence.note: Author's judgement from common maintenance practice.

sources.title: Reliability and O&M key performance indicators of onshore and offshore wind turbines based on field-data analysis (Walgern et al.)
sources.supports: Onshore failure rate 3.3 non-resettable failures per turbine per year (1.729 per MW per year); WMEP onshore 2.4 failures per turbine per year for smaller turbines; average technician time on site 2.7 h for component replacements, about 1.5 h for other corrective maintenance and 3.8 h for preventive maintenance, excluding travel and spare-part lead times; pitch, control and converter systems have the highest onshore failure rates per MW.

sources.title: Working as a wind turbine technician: how to minimise risks
sources.supports: Wind speed limits set by regulations and manufacturers: access to the lower platform up to 25 m/s and to the nacelle up to 20 m/s, hoists below 10 m/s; all work by teams of at least two people; work inside turbines only under a written order or permit; work stops and the team evacuates if gusts threaten stability.

sources.title: Keeping Wind Turbines Spinning (S. Blankinship)
sources.supports: Scheduled wind turbine maintenance is usually done two to three times a year with 12 to 18 hours of downtime per outage; wind farms are often serviced when wind is low; replacement components are expensive and time-consuming to replace; older towers without elevators are climbed.

sources.title: Using Technology to Monitor & Maintain Wind Turbines (J. Martino)
sources.supports: Siemens remote monitoring centres resolve 80 percent of registered alarm cases remotely without a site visit; average response time 10 minutes and 99 percent of alarms answered within an hour; 24/7 remote monitoring centres; vibration-based condition monitoring for early detection.

sources.title: TransAlta Corporation Annual Information Form for the year ended December 31, 2021 (Exhibit 13.1 to Form 40-F)
sources.publisher: TransAlta Corporation via U.S. SEC EDGAR
sources.supports: Alberta wind facility list with capacities and commissioning years: Castle River (1997-2001), Cowley North and Sinnott (2001, five Nordex N60 1.3 MW turbines), McBride Lake (2004, 50 percent), Summerview 1 (2004) and 2, Blue Trail (2009) and Macleod Flats, Soderglen (2006, 50 percent), Oldman (2007), Ardenville (2010), Windrise (206 MW, commercial operation November 2021); wind speeds are historically greater in the cold winter months.

assumptions: touch_min records the lead technician's minutes; the second technician on every climb is counted in the wind_technician FTE (22, about twice the lead's simulated hands-on time of about 7.5 hours per visit times 200 visits a month). Together with scheduled service (about 13 FTE) and main component exchanges (about 2 FTE) this uses about 37 of the 38 technicians in the organisation file, which leaves little room for training, travel between sites and on-call rest and in the wind_tech_pair resource.
The organisation file lists issued_parts from scm-manage-stores as a trigger; parts do not start a visit, so they are shown as a standing input.
roc_operator is added for the remote restart at the end of each repair; the organisation file does not list this role for the process.

Branch shares at diagnosis (74 percent fixed with parts on hand, 19 percent part missing, 6 percent no fault found, 1 percent main component) are estimates; the main component share is set so that escalations (about 1.6 a month) match the organisation file's 1 to 5 exchanges a month.
Cycle time ends when the supervisor closes the work order in a weekly review; time to return to service is given as a separate benchmark.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (wage x 1.40).
Organisation file corrected on 2026-11-24: technicians climb in pairs, so the steps from the drive to the turbine to the drive back now carry people 2, and the staffing check counts both technicians.
